title: Metacarpal bones
source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb (and glossary); 8.5; 9.4; 9.5; 20.5

main.t: The five long bones of the palm, between the wrist and the fingers (metacarpal bones).

simpler.t: The metacarpals are the five bones of your palm.

deeper.t: They are numbered 1 to 5, starting at the thumb.

facts.t: They lie between the carpal bones of the wrist and the bones of the fingers and thumb.
Each base meets a carpal bone of the second row.
Their lower ends form the knuckles, at the base of the fingers.

simpler.t: They make up your palm, from your wrist to your knuckles.

deeper.t: The first metacarpal, at the base of the thumb, is separate from the others.

items.name: Base
items.t: The upper end, which meets a carpal bone at a carpometacarpal joint.

items.name: Shaft
items.t: The long middle part of each bone.

items.name: Head
items.t: The expanded lower end, which forms a knuckle.

items.name: First metacarpal
items.t: Separate from the others, at the base of the thumb; its base forms a saddle joint with the trapezium.

items.name: Second and third metacarpals
items.t: Firmly anchored, so they do not move.

items.name: Fourth and fifth metacarpals
items.t: Can move a little forwards and backwards; the fifth moves most.

simpler.t: Each has a base at the wrist end, a shaft and a head that forms a knuckle.

deeper.t: Each head meets the base of a proximal phalanx at a metacarpophalangeal joint.

facts.t: The first metacarpal is separate, so the thumb can move freely on its own.
The second and third are fixed, giving the palm a firm middle.
The fourth and fifth move forwards in a power grip, pressing the inner hand against the object.

simpler.t: A free thumb bone, a firm middle and movable outer bones help you grip.

items.name: Carpometacarpal joints
items.t: Between the second row of carpal bones and the bases of the metacarpals.

items.name: First carpometacarpal joint
items.t: A saddle joint between the trapezium and the first metacarpal.

items.name: Metacarpophalangeal (knuckle) joints
items.t: Condyloid joints between the metacarpal heads and the proximal phalanges.

items.name: Carpal bones
items.t: The trapezium carries the first and second, and the trapezoid the second. The capitate carries mainly the third, and the hamate the fourth and fifth.

items.name: Palmar arches
items.t: The radial and ulnar arteries join at the wrist to form the palmar arches that supply the hand.

items.name: Palmar venous arches
items.t: The digital veins join in the hand to form the palmar venous arches.

simpler.t: They join the wrist bones above and the finger bones below.

facts.t: They form by replacing a cartilage model with bone (endochondral ossification).
Each has two ossification centres: one for the shaft, and one for the head (in the first, for the base).
facts.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20). Gray’s 1918 (8.2) gives two centres for each metacarpal (supporting only).

facts.t: The first metacarpal ossifies like a phalanx, so some anatomists count the thumb as having three phalanges.
facts.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20). Gray’s 1918 (8.2) gives two centres for each metacarpal (supporting only).

items.injury: A punch that lands on a hard object.
items.damaged: The neck of the fifth metacarpal breaks (“boxer’s fracture”).
items.cannotDo: Make a fist with a normal knuckle: the little-finger knuckle sinks.
items.why: The fifth metacarpal is the most mobile of the palm bones and takes the force of a badly aimed punch.
items.check: The fracture is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20); the mobility of the fifth metacarpal is.

items.injury: A blow along the bent thumb, as in a punch.
items.damaged: The base of the first metacarpal breaks into the saddle joint (Bennett fracture).
items.cannotDo: Pinch or touch the thumb to the fingertips without pain.
items.why: The break enters the saddle joint on which opposition depends.
items.check: The fracture is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20); the saddle joint and opposition are.

items.q: Explain why the thumb’s metacarpal moves so much more than the others.
model: The first metacarpal is separate from the other four.
Its base forms a saddle joint with the trapezium, which is biaxial.
So it moves within the plane of the palm and out in front of it.
Flexion with abduction here produces opposition.

items.q: Compare the movement of the second and third metacarpals with that of the fourth and fifth.
model: The second and third are firmly anchored and immobile.
The fourth and fifth move a little forwards and backwards.
Their forward movement strengthens the grip of the inner hand.

items.q: A man punches a wall and the knuckle of his little finger sinks. Predict the injury and explain it.
model: A fracture of the neck of the fifth metacarpal (boxer’s fracture).
The head tips towards the palm.
So the knuckle sinks when he makes a fist.
The fifth metacarpal is the most mobile and least protected.

check.stem: Which metacarpal is at the base of the thumb?
check.why: The metacarpals are numbered from the thumb: the first is at its base.

check.stem: Which metacarpals are firmly anchored and do not move?
check.why: The second and third are firmly anchored.

options: The second row of carpal bones
The heads (lower ends) of the metacarpals
check.why: The expanded distal end of each metacarpal forms a knuckle.
